title: Delhi High Court Division Bench: A Bank Is Not Automatically Liable Merely Because a Customer Denies Sharing an OTP
case_name: State Bank of India v. Hare Ram Singh & Anr.
citation: LPA 52/2025, neutral citation 2026:DHC:4833-DB, judgment dated 29 May 2026
card_summary: A single judge had directed SBI to compensate a customer for a fraudulent transaction under the RBI's zero liability framework. A Division Bench set that order aside, holding a writ court cannot presume bank deficiency without a technical or forensic examination, and that a bare denial of sharing an OTP does not by itself fix liability where warnings were given and a suspicious link was clicked.
card_tip: Report an unauthorised transaction in writing at once and keep every warning the bank sent beforehand; under the RBI's 2017 circular, where the loss falls depends on that record, not a bare denial made later.
verification_notes: Selected for the Banking & Finance category; cyber fraud liability allocation is a high-demand search topic given rising digital fraud in Delhi NCR, and this Division Bench ruling refines two existing site guides on digital payment fraud liability with the countervailing customer-negligence side of the doctrine, which was not yet covered. Case name, LPA number, neutral citation 2026:DHC:4833-DB and the 29 May 2026 date are confirmed across two independent reports (Bar and Bench, Verdictum). The exact bench composition (names of the two judges) was not confirmed in either source and is therefore not stated.
